topics.nameAr: الوحدة 5: العالم من حولنا (The World Around Us)
topics.description: الحيوانات والطبيعة والطقس + الماضي البسيط والمستمر وصيغ المقارنة/التفضيل.
السفر والأماكن والملابس + المستقبل (will / going to) والأفعال الناقصة (modals).
الشخصية والمشاعر + المضارع التام والمضارع التام المستمر (for/since).
الأحداث وتعابير الزمن + الماضي التام (Past Perfect) لسرد ما حدث قبل حدث آخر.
الصحة والجسم + المضارع التام (ever/never/already/yet) و have to/must.
التكنولوجيا ووسائل الإعلام + الشرط الأول والثاني (Conditionals) و might/may.
البيئة والطبيعة وإعادة التدوير + المبني للمجهول (Passive: present/past simple).
الدول والمهرجانات والمهن + الجمل الموصولة (who/which/where) و (be) able to.
المهن والطموحات + صيغ المستقبل والمبني للمجهول في المستقبل (Future Passive).
المشاعر والقرارات + الشرط الثاني والثالث (Second & Third Conditional).
الأخبار والإعلام + الكلام المنقول (Reported Speech) مع تغيير الأزمنة.
العلوم والاكتشافات + الجمل الموصولة (Relative Clauses) + نصّ سيرة ذاتية.
صفات ful-/less- والمجتمع + أدوات ربط السبب والنتيجة (Cause & Result).
الفنون والمتلازمات (get/take) + مراجعة الأزمنة والمبني للمجهول + كتابة مراجعة.

Where is the old paper taken?
problems.passage: Have you ever wondered what happens to old paper? Every year, millions of tonnes of paper are used around the world. Luckily, paper can be recycled. First, the old paper is collected from homes and schools. Then it is taken to a factory. At the factory, the paper is mixed with water to make a soft grey material. After that, the material is cleaned and pressed into thin sheets. Finally, the sheets are dried and new paper is made. Recycling paper saves trees and energy, so it is very good for our planet.

problems.question: تتبّع استدعاء Factorial(4) وأظهر الاستدعاءات وقيمها (النزول ثم الصعود).
problems.finalAnswer:
النزول (كل استدعاء ينتظر الأصغر):
Factorial(4) = 4 * Factorial(3)
Factorial(3) = 3 * Factorial(2)
Factorial(2) = 2 * Factorial(1)
Factorial(1) = 1 * Factorial(0)
Factorial(0) = 1   ← الحالة الأساسية (توقّف)
الصعود (تعويض القيم الراجعة):
Factorial(1) = 1*1 = 1
Factorial(2) = 2*1 = 2
Factorial(3) = 3*2 = 6
Factorial(4) = 4*6 = 24
النتيجة النهائية: 24

problems.question: تتبّع استدعاء Power(2, 3) للدالة: int Power(int b,int e){ if(e==0) return 1; return b*Power(b,e-1); }
problems.finalAnswer:
النزول:
Power(2,3) = 2 * Power(2,2)
Power(2,2) = 2 * Power(2,1)
Power(2,1) = 2 * Power(2,0)
Power(2,0) = 1   ← الحالة الأساسية
الصعود:
Power(2,1) = 2*1 = 2
Power(2,2) = 2*2 = 4
Power(2,3) = 2*4 = 8
النتيجة النهائية: 8

problems.question: تتبّع استدعاء SumTo(4) للدالة: int SumTo(int n){ if(n==0) return 0; return n+SumTo(n-1); } وأظهر الإطارات.
problems.finalAnswer:
النزول:
SumTo(4) = 4 + SumTo(3)
SumTo(3) = 3 + SumTo(2)
SumTo(2) = 2 + SumTo(1)
SumTo(1) = 1 + SumTo(0)
SumTo(0) = 0   ← الحالة الأساسية
الصعود:
SumTo(1) = 1+0 = 1
SumTo(2) = 2+1 = 3
SumTo(3) = 3+3 = 6
SumTo(4) = 4+6 = 10
النتيجة النهائية: 10

problems.passage: Volunteering is becoming more popular among young people, and this is a very positive change. When teenagers volunteer, they help their community and also learn important skills. For example, some students visit old people who live alone, because these people are often lonely. Others clean parks and beaches, so their towns become cleaner and more beautiful. Volunteering is not always easy; it takes time and energy. However, most young volunteers say that it makes them feel useful and happy. As a result, many schools now encourage their students to volunteer at least once a month.

problems.passage:
THE BRIDGE

Between two lands there stands a bridge,
Across a river deep and wide.
One side is where I used to live,
And new dreams wait on the other side.

I stand upon the bridge and pause,
My old life calling me to stay.
But something stronger pulls me on —
A quiet voice that says, 'This way.'

So step by step I cross the stones,
With fear and hope inside my chest.
For those who never cross the bridge
Will never find what lies ahead.

How many hours of sleep do teenagers need, according to doctors?
problems.passage: TEENAGERS AND SLEEP. Many teenagers do not get enough sleep. Doctors say that young people between 13 and 18 need about nine hours of sleep every night, but most sleep only six or seven hours. There are several reasons for this. First, many teens use their phones late at night. The bright light from the screen makes it harder to fall asleep. Second, teenagers often have a lot of homework and after-school activities, so they go to bed late. When students do not sleep enough, they feel tired and find it difficult to concentrate in class. Some even fall asleep during lessons. Experts give simple advice to help. They suggest turning off phones at least one hour before bed and going to sleep at the same time every night. A short walk or a warm shower in the evening can also help the body relax. Schools in some countries now start lessons later in the morning, and teachers report that students are more awake and learn better. Getting enough sleep is not a luxury — it is an important part of staying healthy.

problems.question: Why can people float easily on the Dead Sea?
problems.passage: THE DEAD SEA. The Dead Sea is one of the most amazing places in Israel. It is a large salt lake, and its surface is the lowest point on Earth — about 430 metres below sea level. The Dead Sea is famous because the water is so salty that people can float on it easily without trying. In fact, it is almost impossible to sink! The salt and minerals in the water are also very good for the skin, so many people come to relax and cover themselves in the black mud from the shore. Every year, thousands of tourists from all over the world visit the Dead Sea. They enjoy floating in the warm water, taking photos and staying in the comfortable hotels nearby. However, the Dead Sea has a serious problem: it is getting smaller every year. The water level is falling because less water flows into it from the Jordan River. Scientists and governments are looking for ways to save this special place, so that future generations can enjoy it too.

problems.question: How old is Ahmad?
problems.passage: A YOUNG HERO. Not all heroes are famous adults. Sometimes, a hero can be an ordinary child. This is the story of Ahmad, a twelve-year-old boy from a small village in the north of Israel. One cold winter afternoon, Ahmad was walking home from school along the river. Suddenly, he heard shouting. A little girl, who had been playing near the water, had fallen into the cold, fast river. Her friends were frightened and did not know what to do. Ahmad did not think twice. He quickly took off his heavy schoolbag and jumped into the water. The river was freezing and strong, but Ahmad was a good swimmer. He reached the girl, held her tightly, and pulled her slowly to the riverbank. Some adults who were passing by helped them both out of the water. The girl was cold and afraid, but she was safe. Later, the girl’s parents came to Ahmad’s house to thank him. They said he was very brave. The mayor of the village also gave Ahmad a special prize for his courage. But Ahmad was modest. "I only did what anyone would do," he said. "I am just happy that she is safe." Ahmad’s story teaches us an important lesson: you do not have to be big or strong to make a difference. Sometimes, all you need is a brave heart and the will to help others.

problems.passage:
THE BRIDGE

Between two lands there stands a bridge,
Across a river deep and wide.
One side is where I used to live,
And new dreams wait on the other side.

I stand upon the bridge and pause,
My old life calling me to stay.
But something stronger pulls me on —
A quiet voice that says, 'This way.'

So step by step I cross the stones,
With fear and hope inside my chest.
For those who never cross the bridge
Will never find what lies ahead.

problems.question: What did Yusuf catch?
problems.passage: THE OLD FISHERMAN (a short story). Every morning, before the sun rose, an old fisherman named Yusuf took his small wooden boat out to sea. He was poor, but he was happy, because he loved the quiet water and the sound of the waves. One day, Yusuf caught a very large and beautiful fish — the biggest he had ever seen. 'I can sell this fish for a lot of money,' he thought. But when he looked into the fish's eyes, he felt sorry for it. The fish was old, like him. After a long moment, Yusuf smiled and gently put the fish back into the sea. 'Go,' he said. 'You deserve to live.' That evening, Yusuf returned home with an empty net and no money. His neighbour laughed at him. 'You are a foolish old man,' he said. But Yusuf did not mind. He knew he had done the right thing. Years later, people in the village still told the story of the kind fisherman who set the great fish free. They said that a good heart is worth more than gold. And Yusuf, though he never became rich, was remembered as the happiest man in the village.

problems.passage:
MY TREE

Outside my window stands a tree,
As tall and old as tall can be.
In spring it wears a coat of green,
The finest coat I have ever seen.

In summer birds come there to rest,
And build their little homes and nest.
In autumn, leaves of gold and red
Fall softly on the flower bed.

In winter, when the cold winds blow,
Its branches wear a hat of snow.
Through every season, rain or sun,
My tree and I are friends — as one.

problems.passage: FROM REFUGEE TO DOCTOR. Dr. Lena Haddad still remembers the day she arrived in a new country as a ten-year-old girl. She spoke no English, had no friends, and missed her old home terribly. Her family had left their country because of war, carrying only a few small bags. 'Those first months were the hardest of my life,' she says. 'I sat at the back of the classroom and understood nothing. I felt invisible.' But Lena was determined not to give up. Every evening, she studied English for hours, watching cartoons and copying words into a notebook. Slowly, she began to understand her teachers and make friends. Her science teacher, Mr. Cohen, noticed how hard she worked and encouraged her to dream big. 'He told me that one day I could become anything I wanted,' Lena recalls. 'I never forgot his words.' Twenty years later, Lena is now a respected doctor who helps sick children in a large hospital. In her free time, she volunteers at a centre for young refugees, teaching them English and giving them hope. 'I know exactly how they feel,' she explains. 'I want them to understand that their difficult start does not decide their future.' Lena's story is a powerful reminder that with hard work, courage and a little kindness from others, even the most difficult beginnings can lead to a bright future.

problems.passage: THE POWER OF VOLUNTEERING. In recent years, more and more young people around the world have started to volunteer their free time to help others. Volunteering means working without payment to support a good cause, and it can take many forms. Some teenagers help elderly people in their neighbourhood, others clean beaches and parks, and some read to young children at the local library. At first, many students volunteer because their school asks them to, or because it looks good on a university application. However, most of them soon discover that volunteering gives them much more than they expected. Studies have shown that people who volunteer regularly feel happier and less stressed. When we help others, our brains release chemicals that improve our mood, so it is good for our mental health. Volunteering also helps young people develop useful skills, such as teamwork, communication and problem-solving. These skills are valuable in almost any future job. In addition, volunteers often make new friends and feel more connected to their community. Of course, volunteering is not always easy. It takes time and energy, and sometimes the work is difficult or even boring. But most volunteers agree that the rewards are worth the effort. As one seventeen-year-old volunteer said, 'When I see the smile on an old man's face, I know that my time was not wasted.' Perhaps that is the greatest reward of all: knowing that you have made a real difference in someone's life.

problems.passage: SHOULD WE STILL LEARN TO WRITE BY HAND? In a world full of computers, tablets and smartphones, some people ask whether children still need to learn to write by hand. After all, most adults now type far more than they write, and some schools have already reduced the number of handwriting lessons. However, many scientists believe that handwriting is still very important, especially for young learners. Research suggests that writing by hand helps the brain in ways that typing does not. When we form letters by hand, several areas of the brain work together, which helps us remember information better. In one well-known study, students who took notes by hand during a lecture remembered more than those who typed their notes on a laptop. This is because writing is slower, so students have to listen carefully and put ideas into their own words, instead of simply copying everything. Handwriting also helps young children learn to read. As they practise forming each letter, they begin to recognise letters more easily and understand how words are built. In addition, handwriting develops fine motor skills — the small, careful movements of the fingers — which are useful for many other tasks. Of course, typing has its advantages too. It is faster, easier to correct, and necessary in the modern workplace. Nobody is suggesting that we should stop using computers. The point is that handwriting and typing are different skills, and both are valuable. Most experts agree that children should learn both. So, the next time you pick up a pen, remember: you are not just writing words on paper — you are also giving your brain a healthy workout.

problems.passage: THE POWER OF VOLUNTEERING. In recent years, more and more young people around the world have started to volunteer their free time to help others. Volunteering means working without payment to support a good cause, and it can take many forms. Some teenagers help elderly people in their neighbourhood, others clean beaches and parks, and some read to young children at the local library. At first, many students volunteer because their school asks them to, or because it looks good on a university application. However, most of them soon discover that volunteering gives them much more than they expected. Studies have shown that people who volunteer regularly feel happier and less stressed. When we help others, our brains release chemicals that improve our mood, so it is good for our mental health. Volunteering also helps young people develop useful skills, such as teamwork, communication and problem-solving. These skills are valuable in almost any future job. In addition, volunteers often make new friends and feel more connected to their community. Of course, volunteering is not always easy. It takes time and energy, and sometimes the work is difficult or even boring. But most volunteers agree that the rewards are worth the effort. As one seventeen-year-old volunteer said, 'When I see the smile on an old man's face, I know that my time was not wasted.' Perhaps that is the greatest reward of all: knowing that you have made a real difference in someone's life.

problems.question: Why did Lena's family leave their country?
problems.passage: FROM REFUGEE TO DOCTOR. Dr. Lena Haddad still remembers the day she arrived in a new country as a ten-year-old girl. She spoke no English, had no friends, and missed her old home terribly. Her family had left their country because of war, carrying only a few small bags. 'Those first months were the hardest of my life,' she says. 'I sat at the back of the classroom and understood nothing. I felt invisible.' But Lena was determined not to give up. Every evening, she studied English for hours, watching cartoons and copying words into a notebook. Slowly, she began to understand her teachers and make friends. Her science teacher, Mr. Cohen, noticed how hard she worked and encouraged her to dream big. 'He told me that one day I could become anything I wanted,' Lena recalls. 'I never forgot his words.' Twenty years later, Lena is now a respected doctor who helps sick children in a large hospital. In her free time, she volunteers at a centre for young refugees, teaching them English and giving them hope. 'I know exactly how they feel,' she explains. 'I want them to understand that their difficult start does not decide their future.' Lena's story is a powerful reminder that with hard work, courage and a little kindness from others, even the most difficult beginnings can lead to a bright future.

problems.passage: THE PAINTING (a short story). Sara had always loved to paint, but she kept her paintings hidden under her bed. She was afraid that people would laugh at them. 'They are not good enough,' she told herself. One day, her art teacher, Mrs. Barak, asked the class to enter a painting in the school competition. Sara wanted to run away. That night, she looked at her favourite painting — a picture of the sea at sunset — and made a brave decision. The next morning, with shaking hands, she gave it to Mrs. Barak. For a whole week, Sara could not sleep. She was sure everyone would laugh. When the day of the results came, she almost stayed at home. But when she walked into the hall, she saw her painting hanging on the wall, with a golden ribbon beside it. She had won first prize. Around her, students were smiling and pointing. 'It's beautiful,' one girl whispered. Sara felt her cheeks turn red, but this time it was from happiness, not fear. Mrs. Barak walked over and put a hand on her shoulder. 'You had this talent all along,' she said gently. 'You just needed the courage to share it.' From that day on, Sara never hid her paintings again. She had learned that the biggest risk is sometimes not trying at all.

I stand upon the bridge and pause,
My old life calling me to stay.
But something stronger pulls me on —
A quiet voice that says, 'This way.'

So step by step I cross the stones,
With fear and hope inside my chest.
For those who never cross the bridge
Will never find what lies ahead.

problems.question: What did Sara win?
problems.passage: THE PAINTING (a short story). Sara had always loved to paint, but she kept her paintings hidden under her bed. She was afraid that people would laugh at them. 'They are not good enough,' she told herself. One day, her art teacher, Mrs. Barak, asked the class to enter a painting in the school competition. Sara wanted to run away. That night, she looked at her favourite painting — a picture of the sea at sunset — and made a brave decision. The next morning, with shaking hands, she gave it to Mrs. Barak. For a whole week, Sara could not sleep. She was sure everyone would laugh. When the day of the results came, she almost stayed at home. But when she walked into the hall, she saw her painting hanging on the wall, with a golden ribbon beside it. She had won first prize. Around her, students were smiling and pointing. 'It's beautiful,' one girl whispered. Sara felt her cheeks turn red, but this time it was from happiness, not fear. Mrs. Barak walked over and put a hand on her shoulder. 'You had this talent all along,' she said gently. 'You just needed the courage to share it.' From that day on, Sara never hid her paintings again. She had learned that the biggest risk is sometimes not trying at all.

According to the text, how does writing by hand help the brain?
problems.finalAnswer: Several areas of the brain work together when we form letters by hand, which helps us remember information better.
problems.passage: SHOULD WE STILL LEARN TO WRITE BY HAND? In a world full of computers, tablets and smartphones, some people ask whether children still need to learn to write by hand. After all, most adults now type far more than they write, and some schools have already reduced the number of handwriting lessons. However, many scientists believe that handwriting is still very important, especially for young learners. Research suggests that writing by hand helps the brain in ways that typing does not. When we form letters by hand, several areas of the brain work together, which helps us remember information better. In one well-known study, students who took notes by hand during a lecture remembered more than those who typed their notes on a laptop. This is because writing is slower, so students have to listen carefully and put ideas into their own words, instead of simply copying everything. Handwriting also helps young children learn to read. As they practise forming each letter, they begin to recognise letters more easily and understand how words are built. In addition, handwriting develops fine motor skills — the small, careful movements of the fingers — which are useful for many other tasks. Of course, typing has its advantages too. It is faster, easier to correct, and necessary in the modern workplace. Nobody is suggesting that we should stop using computers. The point is that handwriting and typing are different skills, and both are valuable. Most experts agree that children should learn both. So, the next time you pick up a pen, remember: you are not just writing words on paper — you are also giving your brain a healthy workout.

problems.passage: LETTER TO THE EDITOR: SAVE OUR LIBRARY. Dear Editor, I am writing to express my concern about the town council's plan to close our local library next year. As a student, I believe this would be a serious mistake that would harm our whole community. First of all, the library is much more than a room full of books. For many students like me, it is a quiet, comfortable place to study, especially for those who do not have space at home. Every afternoon, the reading room is full of young people doing their homework. Where will they go if it closes? Secondly, the library offers free access to computers and the internet. Not every family can afford these at home, so the library helps to make sure that all children have equal opportunities. Closing it would increase the gap between rich and poor families. Some council members argue that the library is too expensive to run and that people can find everything online. However, this is simply not true for everyone. Elderly people, in particular, often depend on the library's help and friendly staff. I understand that the council must save money, but there are surely better ways to do this. Instead of closing the library, why not open it to volunteers, or organise events to raise funds? I urge the council to think again and to listen to the people who use this valuable service every day. Our library is the heart of our community, and once it is gone, we will never get it back. Yours sincerely, Rania Khoury

problems.question: What is one of the main reasons for the growth of electric cars?
problems.passage: THE RISE OF ELECTRIC CARS. Only a few years ago, electric cars were quite rare on our roads. Today, however, they are becoming a common sight, and many experts believe that they will soon replace petrol cars completely. But what has caused this change, and is it really good news? One of the main reasons for the growth of electric cars is concern about the environment. Petrol and diesel cars release harmful gases that pollute the air and contribute to climate change. Electric cars, on the other hand, produce no exhaust gases at all. In cities where thousands of cars drive every day, switching to electric vehicles could greatly improve the quality of the air we breathe. Another reason is cost. Although electric cars are often more expensive to buy, they are much cheaper to run. Electricity costs less than petrol, and electric cars have fewer moving parts, so they need less repair. Over several years, a driver can save a large amount of money. Of course, electric cars are not perfect. One common complaint is that they cannot travel very far before their batteries need charging. In addition, there are still not enough charging stations, especially in the countryside. However, technology is improving quickly. Newer models can travel further on a single charge, and governments around the world are building more charging stations every year. Some countries have even announced that they will ban the sale of new petrol cars in the near future. It seems clear that the age of the electric car has arrived. While there are still problems to solve, the benefits for our health, our environment and our wallets are simply too great to ignore.

What was Elias's job?
problems.passage: THE LIGHTHOUSE KEEPER (a short story). For thirty years, Elias had lived alone in the lighthouse on the edge of the cliffs. Every night, he climbed the two hundred steps to light the great lamp, so that ships could find their way safely home. The villagers rarely saw him, and some of the children believed he was a ghost. But Elias was not lonely. He had the sea, the wind, and the stars for company, and he was proud of his important work. One stormy winter night, the wind howled like a wild animal. Through the rain, Elias saw a small fishing boat struggling against the enormous waves. He knew at once that the men would drown unless someone helped them. Without hesitating, he ran down to the shore, pushed out his own tiny boat, and rowed into the darkness. The sea threw him up and down, and more than once he thought he would not survive. But at last he reached the fishermen and pulled them, one by one, into his boat. When the exhausted men reached the shore, the whole village was waiting. The next morning, the mayor came to thank Elias, but the old keeper only shook his head. 'A lighthouse is not just a lamp,' he said quietly. 'It is a promise. And I have never broken a promise in my life.' From that day on, the children no longer spoke of ghosts. Instead, they spoke of the brave old man who guarded their village from the top of the cliffs.

problems.question: What is one argument in favour of zoos?
problems.passage: SHOULD ZOOS EXIST? Few places attract families more than a zoo. Children press their faces against the glass to watch a sleeping tiger or laugh at the tricks of a clever monkey. Yet in recent years, more and more people have begun to question whether zoos should exist at all. The debate is not a simple one, and there are strong arguments on both sides. Those who support zoos point out that modern zoos are very different from the cruel animal prisons of the past. Today, good zoos play an important role in protecting endangered species. When an animal is close to extinction in the wild, zoos can breed it safely and, in some cases, return its young to their natural habitat. Zoos also carry out valuable scientific research and teach millions of visitors to care about wildlife. For many children who live in cities, a zoo is the only place where they will ever see a real elephant or lion, and this experience may inspire them to protect nature in the future. Critics, however, argue that no cage, however large, can replace the freedom of the wild. Many animals, they say, suffer from boredom and stress when they are kept in enclosures far smaller than their natural territory. Large animals such as elephants and polar bears, which naturally travel great distances, are particularly affected. Some critics also claim that zoos exist mainly to make money, and that education and conservation are simply excuses. They believe that the money spent on keeping animals in captivity would be better used to protect them in their natural homes. So who is right? Perhaps the answer lies not in closing all zoos, but in improving them. A well-run zoo that puts the welfare of its animals first, supports genuine conservation projects and educates the public can do a great deal of good. A badly run zoo that treats animals as mere entertainment cannot be defended. In the end, the question may not be whether zoos should exist, but what kind of zoos we are willing to accept.

problems.passage: SHOULD ZOOS EXIST? Few places attract families more than a zoo. Children press their faces against the glass to watch a sleeping tiger or laugh at the tricks of a clever monkey. Yet in recent years, more and more people have begun to question whether zoos should exist at all. The debate is not a simple one, and there are strong arguments on both sides. Those who support zoos point out that modern zoos are very different from the cruel animal prisons of the past. Today, good zoos play an important role in protecting endangered species. When an animal is close to extinction in the wild, zoos can breed it safely and, in some cases, return its young to their natural habitat. Zoos also carry out valuable scientific research and teach millions of visitors to care about wildlife. For many children who live in cities, a zoo is the only place where they will ever see a real elephant or lion, and this experience may inspire them to protect nature in the future. Critics, however, argue that no cage, however large, can replace the freedom of the wild. Many animals, they say, suffer from boredom and stress when they are kept in enclosures far smaller than their natural territory. Large animals such as elephants and polar bears, which naturally travel great distances, are particularly affected. Some critics also claim that zoos exist mainly to make money, and that education and conservation are simply excuses. problems.passage: THE WOMAN WHO PLANTED A FOREST. When Aisha first returned to her home village after many years in the city, she could hardly believe her eyes. The green hills she remembered from her childhood had turned into a dry, brown desert. The trees had been cut down for firewood and to make space for farming, and without them, the soil had blown away in the wind. The wells had dried up, and many families had left, unable to grow enough food to survive. Most people would have shaken their heads sadly and returned to the city. Aisha, however, decided to act. She had read that trees could bring life back to damaged land, and she was determined to try. With almost no money, she began to collect seeds and plant them, one by one, on the empty hillsides. At first, the villagers laughed at her. 'One woman cannot grow a forest,' they said. But Aisha did not give up. Every morning, before the sun grew too hot, she watered her young trees and protected them from hungry goats. Slowly, the tiny plants grew stronger. As the years passed, something remarkable happened. The first few trees became hundreds, and then thousands. Their roots held the soil in place, and their leaves gave shade and shelter. Birds and insects returned, and the water slowly came back to the wells. Seeing the change, the villagers stopped laughing and began to help. Together, they planted even more trees, until the brown hills were green once again. Today, Aisha's forest covers the land where nothing once grew, and families who had left have started to return. Scientists come from far away to study how one determined person brought a dead landscape back to life. When they ask Aisha for the secret of her success, she simply smiles. 'I did not plant a forest,' she tells them. 'I planted one tree, and then I planted another. That is all anyone can ever do.'
